solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Dodged heartless enemies, like Batman?

indicators.note: a word with no heart has lost its middle, so only its two end letters remain

blocks.note: first and last letters of the word
Batman wears a cape, so he is caped

explanation.surface: A caped crusader slips past his foes in a comic-book scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who dodged danger got away from it, which is the past tense of break free or flee.

clue.text: Fixed rates as well as variable, not the real thing

indicators.note: something fixed has been rearranged or rigged, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: algebra uses x, y and z as unknown variables

explanation.surface: A finance product offers both fixed and variable interest rates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixed rates' reads as a mortgage term, but 'Fixed' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Ersatz describes an inferior substitute or imitation, so it is something other than the genuine article.

clue.text: Name a Republican, boring rotter, making fake news

indicators.note: something boring drills into another thing, so these letters sit inside the next word

blocks.note: a cad is a dishonourable man
standard abbreviation, as in US politics

explanation.surface: Someone names a dull Republican as the villain spreading misinformation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' looks like a dull Republican, but it means drilling into CAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A canard is an unfounded rumour or false story, the older word for deliberately misleading reports.

clue.text: Tommy periodically retypes periodical

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter of the word is taken

blocks.note: Tommy is slang for a British soldier of the lowest rank
the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A soldier types his letters out again every so often.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye is a long-running British satirical magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: A periodical is a magazine issued at regular intervals, and this one appears fortnightly in Britain.

clue.text: Attractive policeman dresses in loincloth

indicators.note: to dress someone is to wrap clothing around them, so the outer word encloses the other

blocks.note: Detective Inspector, a British police rank

explanation.surface: A handsome officer appears wearing only a loincloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A dhoti is the length of cloth wrapped around the waist and legs worn by men in India.

clue.text: Clubs going through a good patch in match

blocks.note: a player on form is enjoying a good run

explanation.surface: A football club enjoys a run of good results during a fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: Match here is a verb, not the sporting fixture the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To conform is to agree with or correspond to a standard, which is a verb sense of match.

clue.text: Sweet food, English jam sandwiches, given hype

indicators.note: a sandwich holds a filling between its outer slices, so one word goes inside the other

blocks.note: to jam is to pack tightly

explanation.surface: English jam sandwiches are promoted as a treat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jam sandwiches' looks like food, but jam means cram and sandwiches puts E inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A cream puff is a choux pastry filled with whipped cream, a sugary confection or dessert.

clue.text: News about those who keep dry bread

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first letters go around the second group

blocks.note: read as N's: two Ns, N being short for new
Alcoholics Anonymous, whose members stay off alcohol

explanation.surface: A report on people who keep things dry.
explanation.walkthrough: Dry here means teetotal; News splits as N's, two Ns placed either side.
explanation.definitionFit: Naan is a leavened flatbread from South Asian cooking, baked in a tandoor oven.

clue.text: One’s excluded work or duties

definitions.note: a description of a person: one who is excluded

indicators.note: to work something is to knead or reshape it, so the letters get rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is left out of the work rota or other tasks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'work' looks like a noun alongside duties, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An outsider is a person not accepted into a group, left on the margins rather than inside.

clue.text: Fool admitted to dodgy drama school for believers

indicators.note: something admitted is let inside, so the first word goes within the others
dodgy means unreliable or crooked, so these letters are out of order

blocks.note: an ass is a silly person

explanation.surface: An idiot gets into a shady theatre school.
explanation.definitionFit: A madrassa is an Islamic religious college where students study the Koran and faith.

clue.text: Egyptian maybe more cheerful deposing monarch

indicators.note: to depose a ruler is to remove them, so the letters for a monarch are taken out

blocks.note: comparative of sunny, bright in mood

explanation.surface: An Egyptian is happier after a king is overthrown.
explanation.walkthrough: Most Egyptians are Sunni Muslims, so 'maybe' marks an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sunni is a member of the largest branch of Islam, the faith of many people in Egypt.

clue.text: Was a ham stuffed, eating cold starter for dinner?

indicators.note: something eating takes food inside it, so the outer word encloses the next letter
a starter comes first, so only the opening letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: Was the ham stuffed, with a cold course before the main meal?
explanation.walkthrough: Ham is the bad actor, not the meat that 'stuffed' and 'dinner' suggest.
explanation.definitionFit: A ham is a showy, exaggerated performer, so playing a part like one is to perform with too much emphasis.

clue.text: It’s not the main change at rare packing company

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so the letters are put in another order
packing means putting something inside, so these letters surround the company

explanation.surface: A business changes how it packs rare goods.
explanation.walkthrough: The main is an old word for the open sea, not 'the main thing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Terra firma is solid dry land, as opposed to the ocean, which poets call the main.

clue.text: Cycling around African country’s capital

indicators.note: cycling means going round in a loop, so letters move from the front to the back

blocks.note: a landlocked state in West Africa

explanation.surface: A cyclist tours the capital of an African nation.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts the capital in Africa, but Lima is in South America.
explanation.definitionFit: Lima is the seat of government and largest city of Peru, its national capital.

clue.text: Profligate, having large liabilities including tiny sum in America

indicators.note: including means holding something within, so the small sum goes inside

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, as on clothing sizes
IOUs are written promises to repay debts
a cent is one hundredth of a dollar; the clue gives no separate signal for the I placed before it

explanation.surface: A spendthrift runs up huge debts in the US, a few dollars at a time.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse comes up one I short: L plus IOUS around CENT gives nine letters, so the extra I goes unexplained, probably a slip by the setter.
explanation.definitionFit: Profligate can mean dissolute and wildly immoral, which matches the sense of sexually unrestrained behaviour.

clue.text: Get serious spite about setter on public transport

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for spite goes around the rest

blocks.note: the setter refers to themselves as I

explanation.surface: A spiteful remark about the crossword setter on a bus.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'setter on transport' puts I after BUS.
explanation.definitionFit: To mean business is an idiom for being earnestly determined and no longer joking.

clue.text: Producer of coinage is let go? No, sacked!

indicators.note: a sacked town is ransacked and thrown into disorder, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone at the Mint is let go — no, worse, sacked!
explanation.walkthrough: Coinage here means inventing words, not minting money.
explanation.definitionFit: A neologist coins new words, and a newly invented term is called a coinage.

clue.text: Part of US county blessed, overlooking lake

indicators.note: to overlook something is to leave it out, so that letter is dropped

blocks.note: Kent is a county in south-east England

explanation.surface: A fortunate part of an American county looks out over a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Kentucky is one of the fifty states of America, a component of the nation.

clue.text: One starting booze, drinking booze before noon

indicators.note: something drinking takes liquid in, so the outer word swallows the others
before places one piece ahead of the next in the order they read

blocks.note: the second booze: beer is an alcoholic drink
the first booze: gin is a spirit

explanation.surface: A drinker starts on booze before midday.
explanation.walkthrough: BEER takes in GIN followed by N.
explanation.definitionFit: A beginner is a novice, someone who is just setting out on a new activity.

clue.text: At times back in love, really get mushy about love

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only its final letter is used
about means surrounding, so the mushy word goes around the zero-like letter

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: Sometimes a reunited couple get sentimental about each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Every so often is an idiom for occasionally, now and then, on some occasions.

clue.text: Excursion is returning, touring a long way away

indicators.note: returning means coming back, so the short word is read the other way
touring means going all round, so those letters surround the distance phrase

explanation.surface: A traveller comes home after touring somewhere far away.
explanation.definitionFit: A safari is an expedition or trip to watch wild animals, especially in Africa.

clue.text: Brittany on vacation? I don’t know the way round

indicators.note: a vacated building has been emptied, so the word loses its interior letters

blocks.note: what a quiz contestant says when unable to answer

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker in Brittany admits being lost.
explanation.walkthrough: Brittany is the French region, natural on holiday, but only its ends are used.
explanation.definitionFit: A bypass is a road that routes traffic around a town rather than through its centre.

clue.text: One put in charge briefly for Labour

indicators.note: put in means placed inside, so the single letter goes within the other word
briefly means cut short, so the last letter of the word is dropped

blocks.note: a toll is a fee to use a road or bridge

explanation.surface: Someone is briefly put in charge of the Labour Party.
explanation.walkthrough: Capitalised Labour suggests the British political party; here it is plain hard work.
explanation.definitionFit: Toil is hard, exhausting physical work, a close synonym of labour as a noun.

clue.text: Boxer defending position completely still

indicators.note: a defender stands around what they protect, so the outer word surrounds the inner

blocks.note: a place, as in 'in his stead'

explanation.surface: A boxer holds his ground without moving.
explanation.definitionFit: Rock-steady means firmly fixed and not wavering at all, as solid as stone.

clue.text: Wiping up sauce boat

indicators.note: wiping something off removes it, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: taken as written; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: Mopping up a gravy boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sauce boat' looks like one item, but boat is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A ketch is a two-masted sailing vessel, a kind of small ship.

clue.text: Berry turned into aphrodisiac artfully

indicators.note: into means found inside, so the answer lies within the following words
turned means facing the other way, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A berry is cleverly made into a love potion.
explanation.definitionFit: Acai is a small purple palm fruit from the Amazon, marketed as a superfood.

clue.text: Impress one doing a sentence by hand

blocks.note: a person's hand is their handwriting

explanation.surface: Writing out a sentence by hand to make a good impression.
explanation.walkthrough: Impress means force into service, not make an impression; sentence is a prison term.
explanation.definitionFit: To impress is to press-gang someone into military service, which is what conscription does.

clue.text: Tennis champion thus going around with alias

indicators.note: going around means turning back on itself, so the short word is read backwards

explanation.surface: A tennis star travels under an assumed name.
explanation.definitionFit: Naomi Osaka is a Japanese player who has won several Grand Slam singles titles.

clue.text: King in dubious history losing face — Richard III?

indicators.note: a face is the front, so losing it drops the opening letter
in places the king's letter inside the remaining letters
dubious means doubtful or suspect, so the letters are untrustworthy and out of order

blocks.note: the word minus its first letter

explanation.surface: A king whose history is doubtful loses face: Richard III, villain or victim?
explanation.walkthrough: Richard III was the last king from the House of York; the question mark flags an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yorkist is a supporter or member of the House of York in the Wars of the Roses, as Richard III was.

clue.text: Jeer receiving writer’s tip for facetious title

indicators.note: receiving means taking in, so the jeer encloses the other piece

explanation.surface: A writer is jeered while receiving a tip.
explanation.definitionFit: His Nibs is a jokey mock-honorific for a self-important man, like calling him His Lordship.
